samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick a tight set, give every item a yardstick and flag the stale-cardholder and budget-phasing traps. B explains its comparison choices more fully (seasonality, uneven costs, a target for holds) and adds a useful caveat about branch hours. Its reason for dropping cost per visit is also sharper. A covers the money question a bit more through cost per visit, but its branch note is muddled, and B's renumbering of the original list is only a minor flaw. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick a similar, well-sized set, give each item a comparison basis, and explain what they leave off. A gives fuller reasons, such as cost per visit penalizing digital use and programs, and adds useful caveats about lumpy spending and branch hours, though its money side rests on the budget line alone. B covers money more evenly by adding cost per visit, but that measure comes with no caveat, and its branch advice is muddled ('all four branches in one line' versus system totals only).

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick 7 measures, give a reason for each of the 7 left off, and cover both service and money. A is stronger on the misleading-measure item: it says to count only active cards for cardholders and to phase the budget plan by month so lumpy costs don't look like overspending. B never caveats inactive cards in its cardholder share. A also explains why each comparison was chosen, while B mostly gives that reasoning in its design notes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick a well-sized set of 7, give each measure a sensible comparison basis and cover both service and money. B does more on measures that can mislead: it counts only cardholders active in the last 2–3 years so dead cards don't inflate the total, and it compares spending to a month-by-month plan so lumpy costs don't look like overspending. A's caveats are limited to seasonality and cost-per-visit noise.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick a small set, explain the seasonal comparison and cover the layout well. B is ahead on the money question: it adds cost per visit on a rolling 12 months and adjusts the budget plan for bills that arrive in lumps. It also defines active cardholders precisely, while A's 'percent of town' still seems to count inactive cards. A gives slightly stronger reasons for what it leaves off and a richer layout, but those don't outweigh B's better caveats on misleading measures and its fuller treatment of finances. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick a short list, give each measure a sensible yardstick and explain why same-period-last-year comparisons handle seasonality. A covers the money question better: it adds a rolling 12-month cost per visit alongside budget vs plan, and it fixes the inactive-cardholder problem by counting only cards used in the last 12 to 24 months. B points out the inactive-card flaw but then uses a percentage of the town that still includes inactive cards, and it has only one finance measure, though its layout advice is very practical.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain the real problem well: 12 tiles were lit at once, so the real outage didn't stand out, and brighter red would just make all 12 louder. B gives more specific fixes (showing values instead of just colours, a 'what's breaking now' strip, flagging tiles that stop updating) and a sharper pre-meeting check. However, it cites a 'well-documented' effect without a source, calls the outage day 'a normal day', and is longer with more technical terms. A is shorter, sticks to the user's numbers and is easier for a non-technical director to follow, so it edges ahead. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain clearly that 12 lit tiles made the real outage hard to spot. Both give concrete fixes: make red rare, rank the tiles, and page someone for critical alerts. B is slightly better for this audience because its tips on how to persuade the director are more useful (start by agreeing with his instinct, don't call the other 11 tiles meaningless) and it gives a measurable goal and a practice drill. A has more useful pre-meeting checks but includes some more technical items. A also says the effect is 'well-documented' without naming any source.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain the real cause well (too many red tiles make the important one look normal) and recommend similar concrete fixes. B does more to let the director check the claim himself: it asks how many tiles are non-green on a typical day, how many of the 11 were truly urgent, and whether a page went out, and it adds a 'Needs attention' strip and answers to his likely objections. A is tighter and easier for a non-technical reader, but its checks are aimed at the user more than the director, and it overreaches slightly by saying a third of the board is 'always' in a warning state and by promising detection in 'a few' minutes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain the noise problem clearly and give concrete fixes, with similar analogies and scripts. A does better at giving something checkable: it suggests counting how many tiles are non-green on a typical day and how many of the 11 were actually urgent. B's script promises detection will drop 'from 25 minutes to a few', which is a figure it has no basis for. B is a little tighter, but A's pushback section and verification checklist make it more useful for the meeting.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain the cause clearly, recommend similar concrete fixes and use a car-dashboard analogy. Both suggest checking how many tiles are non-green on a normal day, but neither suggests replaying last month's outage. B is tighter and gives a ready-to-use script, but it adds an outside statistic (1 in 12 men are colorblind) and states 'on a normal day plenty of tiles are red or amber' as fact before it is checked. A keeps its invented figures clearly illustrative and flags its estimates as unverified, which gives it the edge. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain clearly that brighter red makes all 12 lit tiles louder without making the real outage easier to spot, and both use a car-dashboard analogy. B's recommendations are more specific: it suggests fixing thresholds against normal levels, adding a 'needs attention' strip ranked by impact, and making healthy tiles quiet. B also adds fewer outside figures, leaving the time-to-notice target for the user and director to set, while A brings in an outside colorblindness statistic. A is shorter and easier for a non-technical reader, but B's more concrete plan and clearer advice on what to check before the meeting give it the edge.
